name: Augustine of Hippo
role: Bishop of Hippo and Christian theologian (354-430)
summary: Augustine held that earthly states are needed to keep a fallen world in peace but are just only insofar as they serve justice, and that all power comes from God. He defended the use of imperial law to compel Donatists and suppress idolatry, accepted slavery and the subordination of wife to husband as consequences of sin, and allowed just war as a sad necessity while condemning conquest for its own sake.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He tells the general Boniface that one can please God in active military service and that war may be waged as a necessity to secure peace, and rejects the claim that Christianity demands pacifism.

assisted-dying.rationale: He argues that no divine precept allows anyone to take a life, including one's own, and that the commandment against killing covers every human being, which leaves no room for a physician to end a patient's life.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: He says offences against nature, such as those of the men of Sodom, are to be everywhere and always detested and punished, without saying who is to punish them.

death-penalty.rationale: He holds that those who put wicked men to death on public authority do not break the commandment, but in Letter 133 he asks a judge to spare the lives of convicted Circumcellions.

destroy-worshipped-objects.rationale: He holds up Hezekiah and Josiah, who destroyed idols, groves and temples, as kings who served God in that office, and says imperial laws against idolatry are rightly enacted.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: He states that the power of giving kingdoms and empires belongs to no one but the true God, who grants royal power to the pious and impious as he wills.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He holds that by nature no one is the slave of another, yet accepts slavery and the master's rule as just consequences of sin, so his record points both ways.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: He says animals, being without reason, are subjected by the Creator's just appointment for us to kill or keep alive for our own uses.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: He cites the scriptural kings Hezekiah, Josiah and Nebuchadnezzar as models of rulers who serve God by enacting laws that enforce righteousness and punish the opposite.

leader-cult.rationale: He warns rulers not to be puffed up by praise and obsequious honours, and praises the emperor who is humble before God.

more-religion-public.rationale: In his letter on the correction of the Donatists and in Letter 93 he argues that kings serve God as kings by enforcing laws against impiety, and he praises Christian emperors who use their power to extend the worship of God.

national-church-status.rationale: He supports imperial laws that confiscate the property of schismatics and favour the Catholic Church's unity over the Donatists, though he speaks of one universal Church rather than a national one.

natural-rulers.rationale: He says God did not intend man to rule over man by nature, only over beasts, and that rule over men came with sin.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: He calls obeying princes a general compact of human society and says Christians obey the laws of the earthly city that govern mortal life, though God is to be obeyed above any ruler.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: He cites Christ's answer on putting away a wife, that what God has joined man must not put asunder, as the foundation of marriage.

premarital-sex.rationale: He confesses his own fornications as sin and teaches that sexual intercourse belongs only within marriage, for procreation.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: He approves Nebuchadnezzar's law against blaspheming God as a way a king serves the Lord and defends the Christian emperors' laws against idolaters and schismatics.

reason-over-faith.rationale: He describes how he came to accept that belief in Scripture and the testimony of others is necessary, since life itself rests on things believed without demonstration.

rehabilitation.rationale: In Letter 133 he asks that the guilty be corrected by lawful coercion and made to take up useful labour, calling that discipline a benefit rather than vindictive punishment.

religions-one-truth.rationale: He argues against Porphyry that the Christian religion alone holds the universal way of deliverance of the soul and that none can be delivered except by it.

sacred-ruler.rationale: He says Christian emperors are happy only if they remember they are men and do not let themselves be lifted up by those who pay them sublime honours.

separate-church-state.rationale: He rejects the objection that the apostles never sought help from kings and holds that rulers must now use the law to protect the Church and punish error, so he does not separate the two.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: He describes the ordered household as one where the husband rules the wife, the parents the children and masters the servants, although rulers should govern out of duty rather than love of power.

spiritual-nature.rationale: He says Christian rulers should use their power to extend the worship of God and that the heavenly city uses earthly peace so that an unhindered religious life is possible.

state-harmful.rationale: He treats civil order and earthly peace as a real, usable good and says a wise man will serve as a judge because human society requires it, though he calls states without justice great robberies.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He calls crushing neighbours who do no harm through mere lust of dominion great robbery, and says it is greater felicity to have a good neighbour at peace than to conquer a bad one.

traditional-family.rationale: He calls the household the beginning or element of the city, so that domestic concord of rule and obedience underlies civic order.

universal-morality.rationale: He says the law written in human hearts survives even wickedness and that offences against nature are to be detested and punished everywhere and at all times.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: He allows the contemplative, active or mixed life but says no one may be so absorbed in leisure as to forget the service owed to a neighbour.

notes: Searched the City of God, Confessions, the Donatist writings and Letters 93, 133, 138 and 189 for state and law, war, coercion, punishment, property, poverty, slavery, family, marriage, sexuality, animals and religion, and read the SEP entry. Texts not in the local library (De libero arbitrio, Letter 185 in full, sermons, the anti-Pelagian and marriage treatises) were not read, so statements on property, unjust law, abortion and marriage law are left null. Some answers rest on 4th-5th century positions applied to modern statements only where his own text addresses the same question.
